title: Fire on Carmel (1 Kings 18:20–39)
hookLine: how long will you limp between two opinions? water-soaked wood, and fire falls

cards: "How long halt ye between two opinions?" Halt is an older English word for limp. How long will you limp along, one foot on each side?
Elijah says it on Mount Carmel, to a crowd of his own people, gathered by the king. On one side stand the prophets of Baal, the god the king and queen have favored. On the other, Elijah, alone.
"If the LORD be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him." And the line that hangs in the air: "the people answered him not a word."

teach.h: THE GOD THAT ANSWERETH BY FIRE.
teach.b: Elijah proposes a test. Two altars, two bulls, wood, and no fire. "The God that answereth by fire, let him be God."

The people finally speak: "It is well spoken." The prophets of Baal go first, calling from morning until noon, and on into the afternoon. The report is short: "there was no voice, nor any that answered."

teach.h: TWELVE STONES, AND WATER, THREE TIMES.
teach.b: Then Elijah repairs the altar of the LORD that had been broken down, with twelve stones, one for each tribe of the sons of Jacob, in a kingdom now split in two.
Then he has water poured over the offering and the wood, and again, and a third time, until it fills the trench.
His prayer is short: "Hear me, O LORD, hear me, that this people may know that thou art the LORD God, and that thou hast turned their heart back again."
In the line before, he asks that Israel know he is God's servant, yes, but the prayer ends on the people: their hearts, turned back. And the fire falls.

It "consumed the burnt sacrifice, and the wood, and the stones, and the dust, and licked up the water that was in the trench." The people fall on their faces: "The LORD, he is the God; the LORD, he is the God."
The silence has become an answer. The chapter goes on to a grim ending at the brook Kishon, and readers have wrestled with it.
But at its center is the question Elijah asked first, about limping: a life with one foot on each side, never quite choosing.

how: Some Christians read Elijah on Mount Carmel in sermons on wholehearted faith, and his question about halting between two opinions is sometimes quoted when preachers speak about indecision.

s: Elijah soaked his own altar with water before he prayed
water was poured on the offering and the wood three times, until it filled the trench (18:33–35).
the people answered Elijah's question right away
"the people answered him not a word."
the fire burned only the offering
it consumed the sacrifice, the wood, the stones and the dust, and licked up the water (18:38).

games.q: you're Elijah. your altar is built, the offering is on the wood, and everyone is waiting for fire. what do you do before you pray?
o: light a small flame, just to help it along.
have water poured over everything, three times.
wait until dark, when a fire is easier to see.
games.why: he drenches it until the trench is full. then he prays a short prayer, and the fire licks up even the water.

practice: Bring to mind one decision you've been circling for a while, a conversation to have or not, a commitment to keep or end, and notice the limp: one foot on each side.
You don't have to settle it now; just name the very next step that would end the waiting. If you pray, you can bring the decision before God.

wordCard.voice: Carmel. The mountain where Elijah asked a silent crowd how long they'd limp between two opinions, soaked his altar, prayed, and watched the fire fall.

orig.note: Hebrew: how long, the first words of Elijah's question on Carmel (1 Kings 18:21).
